The type is restrained and fits the world: small engraved-style serif credits, each paired with a tiny heraldic sigil, and a metallic logotype set in the brass band at the end

Real print texture: aged paper, gold foil bands, engraved crest and eagle, a retriever spot illustration, slightly mis-registered colour

tells: A single silhouette-chase idea carries across every frame: the hero, the dog and the pursuers move through settings that keep changing (park gates, docks, an alley seen from above, a hypnotic spiral, a moonlit rooftop), so the frames read as a planned sequence rather than a repeated layout
Each frame has its own unusual palette (dusty rose, teal and ochre, bruised purple, acid green, burnt orange on black, slate blue), yet they share one printed, mid-century look
Credits are part of the scene: one name lies in perspective on the alley floor, another sits inside the illustrated world, and a hand-drawn humanist sans gives the type character
The camera changes a lot: a top-down alley, a flat profile chase, a deep vortex, a wide dockside. That suggests real choreography and rhythm
Real texture: paper grain, painted clouds, rim-lit lamps, and cast shadows that are separate characters
Surprises keep coming: the white dog as a recurring accent, the spiral gag, the rocket silhouette
gaps: The lower-credit frames (VFX supervisor, editor) go back to fairly conventional centred credit blocks over the art; they could have been built into the scene the way 'Andy Serkis' was

tells: A specific, memorable idea: the world is a clockwork map that builds itself, with cities unfolding mechanically on parchment. It works as both a map and a map of the story
Physically convincing materials: hammered brass, carved bone or wood, parchment, and a sun burning out through an armillary sphere. The light is driven by a single blazing source
Shallow depth of field and tilt-shift miniature lensing put a real camera move across a tabletop world
Every frame differs in scale and subject (a band seen from above, a city, a gear tower, an astrolabe, the flat map, the logo crest), yet all stay in one material system
The credits use small engraved caps with a sigil glyph, kept quiet so the mechanism leads, and the title lockup sits inside the metal crest
The sequence is clearly choreographed: it travels from place to place and pivots on the astrolabe
gaps: The credit typography is very small and decorative; legibility is sacrificed, and the type is the least inventive part of the piece
The palette sits almost entirely in sepia, brass and fire, with little tonal surprise across the sequence
The final logo frame leans on bloom and lens flare, which is more conventional than the mechanical invention before it

defects: Most credit cards are static holds that only cut; in the pairs, the 'WRITTEN & DIRECTED BY' frames 1/6 s apart are nearly identical, with no in-shot motion
The pace comes almost entirely from hard cuts (median 0.47s). Nothing carries motion across a cut: no match cuts, no shared vectors, no easing visible between cards

The title holds for 4.2s with only letters dropping out one by one. It reads as a subtractive switch-off, not a choreographed move, and the empty gaps ('NIG CH US') look like missing assets rather than a composed end frame
The RGB-split / chromatic offset on ISAK LINDQVIST and on the title's T and R is a stock glitch effect at default strength
The soundtrack is mostly broadband clicks on cuts plus a white-noise riser (about 6.0–8.4s) with thin, static low tonal partials. There is little musical arrangement or bespoke sound design
The riser drops abruptly at 8.4s into an even bed with no distinct impact layer or low-end hit to sell the title landing
gaps: Motion: this is a slideshow of typographic treatments, not choreography. Top studio work would build each style through in-shot motion (moiré rings that pulse, halftone dots that scale in, LED cells that light up in sequence) and pass energy from card to card with match moves instead of hard cuts

Sound: clicks and a noise riser stand in for a score. It needs a real arrangement (a 'chorus' of voices or instruments, one per typographic style, layering into the title) with designed impacts and a low-end payoff on the reveal

Finish and system: the 'many styles become one title' idea has no thread binding it together (palette, grid, scale and grain all vary freely), and the ending dissolves the title into gaps without settling or rhyming with the opening moiré card
